title: PHALAR: Phasors for Learned Musical Audio Representations
claim: Mapping temporal alignment to rotation in the complex plane lets equal relative timing share the same phase regardless of absolute time.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; spectrogram with markers beside 3D helix polar plot
description: The figure has two panels. On the left is a viridis-colored spectrogram over about one second of music, with horizontal harmonic bands and vertical note onsets. Three red dashed vertical lines labeled 1, 2 and 3 mark timesteps that sit at the same offset from successive note onsets. On the right is a 3D time-expanded polar plot. A vertical Time (s) axis rises from the origin. A learned complex feature traces a helix that revolves around it, with color shifting from dark blue through purple and orange to yellow as time advances. Angle labels run from 0° to 315°, and radial rings mark magnitude. Red boxes labeled 1, 2 and 3 on the helix show the points at the matching timesteps. They land at the same phase angle at different heights. The eye goes first to the colorful helix.
caption: Emergent Phase-Equivariance. Our model’s Learned Spectral Pooling layer maps temporal alignment to geometric rotation in the complex plane. Left: Three timesteps (1, 2, 3) at identical offsets from note onsets. Right: Time-expanded polar plot of a learned feature. As time progresses, the feature revolves around the origin. Because the model is phase-equivariant, positions with the same relative timing (red boxes) share the same phase angle regardless of their absolute time. This allows PHALAR to resolve rhythmic coherence where standard magnitude-based models fail.
abstract: Stem retrieval, the task of matching missing stems to a given audio submix, is a key challenge currently limited by models that discard temporal information. We introduce PHALAR, a contrastive framework achieving a relative accuracy increase of up to $\approx 70\%$ over the state-of-the-art while requiring $<50\%$ of the parameters and a 7$\times$ training speedup. By utilizing a Learned Spectral Pooling layer and a complex-valued head, PHALAR enforces pitch-equivariant and phase-equivariant biases. PHALAR establishes new retrieval state-of-the-art across MoisesDB, Slakh, and ChocoChorales, correlating significantly higher with human coherence judgment than semantic baselines. Finally, zero-shot beat tracking and linear chord probing confirm that PHALAR captures robust musical structures beyond the retrieval task.
